Floating-point addition is not associative because modern computers represent real numbers with finite precision. Under standards such as IEEE 754, a floating-point value has a fixed number of significant binary digits and a limited exponent range. When two values are added, the exact mathematical result usually cannot be represented in that format, so the hardware rounds it to a nearby representable value. Consequently, each addition may discard a small amount of information.

This rounding makes the order of operations matter. Mathematically, adding a, b, and c as (a + b) + c gives the same result as a + (b + c). In floating-point arithmetic, the first addition in each expression is rounded before the second addition occurs. If a is very large and b is much smaller, adding b to a may have no effect because b lies below the representable spacing around a. Yet b might first combine with c to produce a value large enough to affect a. Cancellation between nearly equal values can also expose or amplify rounding errors. Thus, two valid evaluation orders can produce slightly different answers, and in extreme cases the difference can be substantial.

Large matrix multiplication repeatedly computes dot products. Each output entry is a sum of many products. Although the mathematical sum has no preferred order, high-performance implementations divide the work into blocks and distribute partial sums across vector lanes, processor cores, or GPU threads. A serial implementation might accumulate terms from left to right, while a parallel implementation may form many partial sums and combine them through a tree reduction. Different tile sizes, thread counts, scheduling decisions, hardware architectures, compiler optimizations, or numerical libraries can therefore change the reduction order.

Because every partial addition can round differently, these implementations need not produce bit-for-bit identical matrix entries, even when they use the same input data and nominal floating-point format. Fused multiply-add instructions can introduce another difference because they compute a product and addition with only one final rounding, whereas separate multiplication and addition usually round twice. The discrepancies are often tiny, but they can grow with long reductions, poorly scaled data, or severe cancellation. They may also propagate through later computations, especially iterative algorithms or decisions based on thresholds.

Reproducibility therefore requires more than using the same precision. It may require a fixed reduction tree, deterministic scheduling, controlled compiler and library settings, or specialized reproducible summation methods. Higher precision, pairwise summation, and compensated summation can reduce error, but they do not automatically guarantee identical results across different execution orders.
